chapters.beat: Voss is excited in the wrong way — he wants to co-author the eventual report and suggests bringing in a second team for 'methodological rigor'; Tayak understands this as a move to dilute her authority over the site; she agrees to nothing and hangs up furious; she calls Wren and tells her to document everything twice.
chapters.title: Voss Calls [Present — 2024]
chapters.arc_point: Institutional pressure introduced
chapters.bridge_from_prior: Marcus, after the council meeting, has called Voss at the university to report the find — Tayak learns of this call when Voss phones her.

chapters.beat: Wren writes her private field notes — more detailed than the official log; she has sketched the bead and begun researching the 1680s colonial records for Charles County; she finds a land grant document that mentions a 'Piscataway settlement' on the exact coordinates of the mound; she does not yet know whose family that was; she does not yet know it is her own.
chapters.title: Wren's Notes [Present — 2024]
chapters.arc_point: Secondary character established with her own agenda
chapters.bridge_from_prior: Tayak's instruction to document everything twice has sent Wren back to the archive — she is following up on the bead's provenance.

chapters.act: Act I | Past timeline — Saya's era
chapters.beat: 1697: Saya stands in the colonial assembly hall in Annapolis — the only woman, the only Piscataway, in a room of forty men; she reads her petition aloud; the assembly votes to table it pending further survey; Saya presses her handprint in ink beside her signature on the copy she keeps; she walks out into the street and does not cry; she has already decided what to do next.
chapters.title: The Petition [Past — 1695–1697]
chapters.arc_point: Past: Saya's legal fight reaches its crisis
chapters.bridge_from_prior: The petition Saya was drafting in chapters 6–7 has now been completed and submitted — this chapter dramatizes the assembly hearing.

chapters.beat: Kimi posts a video about the excavation to her 80,000 followers — beautiful, passionate, accurate — without telling Tayak; the video goes modestly viral in Indigenous heritage circles; by morning a reporter from the Washington Post has emailed the tribal council; Tayak is not pleased; Kimi is not sorry; this is the beginning of a problem.
chapters.title: Kimi Posts [Present — 2024]
chapters.arc_point: Public dimension of the fight introduced
chapters.bridge_from_prior: Kimi has seen Tayak's permit announcement on the tribal council's internal newsletter — the same document Marcus distributed after chapter 8's meeting.

chapters.act: Act I | Past timeline — Saya's era
chapters.beat: Okwi wraps the petition document in oilskin and carries it to the mound at night; he does not tell Saya; he buries it at the mound's surface layer alongside the glass bead Saya left him when she died the previous winter of a fever; he speaks no ceremony over it — he is not a ceremonial man; he says 'Someone will find this'; he does not know if he believes it; he goes home and does not sleep.
chapters.title: Okwi Buries the Document [Past — 1697]
chapters.arc_point: Past: the artifact's burial — the moment that creates Stratum One
chapters.bridge_from_prior: Saya's petition has failed — Okwi's response is the act that creates the archaeological record Tayak will find 327 years later.

chapters.beat: Tayak uncovers a folded piece of oilskin containing a fragment of a colonial-era document; in the university lab under UV light it resolves as a 1697 petition to the Maryland colonial assembly, signed by a Piscataway woman — the ink is faded but the handprint beside the signature is clear; Tayak photographs it seventeen times and calls Marcus; she does not yet know the name on the document.
chapters.title: Stratum One: The Colonial Document [Present — 2024]
chapters.arc_point: Second artifact; first concrete evidence of legal significance
chapters.bridge_from_prior: The Post reporter's inquiry has reached Slade at the state preservation office — Tayak learns Slade is now monitoring the dig; she returns to the site with this pressure added.

chapters.beat: Slade is polite, thorough, and immediately invokes the permit clause: the 1697 petition qualifies as a document of 'significant historical value' and must be transferred to state custody for analysis; Tayak refuses; Slade does not argue — he simply notes the refusal in his own log and leaves; this is worse than an argument.
chapters.title: Slade Arrives [Present — 2024]
chapters.arc_point: Antagonist enters the field
chapters.bridge_from_prior: The document's significance has reached Slade through the university's required disclosure to the state — he arrives at the site the next morning.

chapters.act: Act I | Past timeline — Saya's era
chapters.beat: 1697–1710: Saya does not stop; she teaches her daughter to read the colonial documents, to understand the legal language, to find the gaps; she teaches her the names of every ancestor she knows, in order, going back as far as the names go; she teaches her the mound — its layers, its meaning, what is buried there and why; her daughter listens; Saya dies in 1710, the same fever that took Okwi two years earlier; her daughter is seventeen and knows everything Saya knew.
chapters.title: Saya's Daughter [Past — 1697–1710]
chapters.arc_point: Past: Saya's legacy — what she passed on
chapters.bridge_from_prior: The petition document Okwi buried was Saya's — this chapter shows what Saya did after the petition failed, and what she gave her daughter.

chapters.beat: Nora sits alone with a quilt she has been making for thirty years — its central panel contains a pattern she has never shown anyone, a map stitched in thread of the mound's interior chambers, learned from her grandmother Ida who learned it from her grandmother before her; she knows what Tayak will find at each layer; she has always known; she picks up the phone to call Tayak and puts it down again; she is not ready; she is afraid of what ready will cost.
chapters.title: Nora's Quilt [Present — 2024]
chapters.arc_point: First hint of Nora's secret — the quilt as oral tradition made visible
chapters.bridge_from_prior: Tayak has phoned Nora to tell her about the 1697 petition — Nora's response on the phone was silence; this chapter shows us why.

chapters.beat: Marcus tells Tayak she can accelerate the recognition petition by submitting the 1697 document to the state voluntarily — it would demonstrate good faith and likely fast-track the legal process; but submitting it means surrendering custody of the most important artifact she has ever found to a system that has historically used such submissions to bury rather than honor Indigenous claims; Tayak cannot decide; she goes back to the mound instead.
chapters.title: The Moral Complication [Present — 2024]
chapters.arc_point: Protagonist's first moral crisis
chapters.bridge_from_prior: Slade's refusal to back down has forced Tayak to consider her options — Marcus has suggested one she does not like.

chapters.beat: A ceramic pipe bowl, Piscataway manufacture, circa 1740s; Tayak photographs it and calls Nora that evening; Nora says 'I know whose that was — that's Matta's; my grandmother Ida told me about him'; Tayak asks how Ida knew; Nora says 'Because Matta's granddaughter told her grandmother, and it came down that way — sit down, there's more'; Tayak realizes the oral history is a chain, each link a person who told the next person, and Nora holds the whole chain.
chapters.title: Stratum Two: The Ceramic Pipe Bowl [Present — 2024]
chapters.arc_point: Third artifact; descent deepens; mound-as-vault hypothesis forms
chapters.bridge_from_prior: Tayak returned to the mound at the end of chapter 18 — she is still there, digging, using the work to avoid the decision.

chapters.act: Act II — early | Past timeline — bridge era
chapters.beat: 1962: Ida is 64 and has been diagnosed with a heart condition she has not told her family about; she calls Nora, then 20, to her kitchen table one night and begins to speak; she tells her about Matta, about Tessa, about the mound's layers, about the names going back further than Ida herself can trace; she tells Nora 'I got this from my grandmother, who got it from hers — you are the next one; don't wait as long as I did'; Nora listens until dawn; Ida dies two years later; Nora has been waiting sixty years to pass it on.
chapters.title: Ida's Night [Past — 1962]
chapters.arc_point: The oral tradition chain dramatized — Ida passes the history to Nora
chapters.bridge_from_prior: Nora's reference to Ida in chapter 19 — this chapter dramatizes the night in 1962 when Ida told Nora everything.

chapters.act: Act II — early | Past timeline — Matta's era
chapters.beat: 1738: Matta attends the colonial church on Sunday morning and leads a traditional ceremony on Sunday evening; he is very good at both; a new colonial ordinance has been posted in the county seat — 'heathen implements' found in Indigenous households are subject to confiscation; Matta reads it twice and begins to plan.
chapters.title: The Double Life [Past — 1738]
chapters.arc_point: Past: Matta's world established; the threat to ceremony introduced
chapters.bridge_from_prior: Nora's story about Matta in chapter 19, grounded in Ida's account — this chapter dramatizes Matta's life.

chapters.act: Act II — early | Past timeline — Matta's era
chapters.beat: Matta begins teaching Tessa the burial map — not written down, never written down, but spoken and walked and repeated until it is in her body; he also teaches her the pipe-making craft; he does not tell her he is dying; she knows anyway; she does not tell him she knows; they work in a comfortable, grieving silence.
chapters.title: Matta and His Granddaughter [Past — 1738–1742]
chapters.arc_point: Past: Matta's relationship with Tessa; the transmission of knowledge
chapters.bridge_from_prior: Matta's plan from chapter 21 — hiding the ceremonial objects — requires a successor who knows where they are buried.

chapters.beat: The Post story quotes an 'anonymous tribal source' saying the mound contains 'proof of a direct bloodline connection to the Piscataway founding families' — something no one has said publicly and that Tayak has not yet established scientifically; Tayak calls Kimi and the conversation is the worst they have ever had; Slade's office issues a formal inquiry within the hour.
chapters.title: Kimi's Mistake [Present — 2024]
chapters.arc_point: New dramatic problem: public pressure backfires
chapters.bridge_from_prior: The Post reporter, energized by Kimi's viral video, has now published a story — Kimi reads it on her phone and realizes it contains a detail she did not authorize.

chapters.beat: Slade drafts a formal notice requiring Tayak to cease excavation pending a review of whether the site qualifies for federal NAGPRA protections — which would, paradoxically, halt the dig that is producing the evidence of those very protections; he pauses before signing it; he signs it; he goes home and tells his wife about his day and leaves out the part he is not proud of.
chapters.title: Slade's Inquiry [Present — 2024]
chapters.arc_point: Institutional pressure escalates
chapters.bridge_from_prior: Slade's inquiry is a direct consequence of the Post story — he is now in his office, drafting it.

chapters.act: Act II — early | Past timeline — Matta's era
chapters.beat: 1743: Matta carries the community's ceremonial objects to the mound at night — the pipe bowl, two carved figures, a bundle of prayer sticks — and buries them in the second stratum, below Okwi's oilskin layer; he speaks the ceremony over each object; he tells Tessa, watching from the tree line, the exact location; he says 'When it is safe, you will know'; she says 'How will I know when it is safe?'; he says 'You won't — you'll have to decide'; he dies six weeks later.
chapters.title: The Hiding [Past — 1743]
chapters.arc_point: Past: Matta buries the ceremonial objects — the act that creates Stratum Two
chapters.bridge_from_prior: The colonial confiscation ordinance from chapter 21 is now being enforced — Matta must act.

chapters.beat: Tayak calls Marcus in a fury; Marcus explains the paradox calmly: NAGPRA protects Indigenous remains but requires a federally recognized tribe to invoke it — and the Piscataway are not federally recognized; the law designed to help them cannot reach them; Tayak has 48 hours to respond to Slade's notice or lose the permit entirely; she goes to Nora's house and sits in the kitchen and does not speak for twenty minutes.
chapters.title: NAGPRA [Present — 2024]
chapters.arc_point: Legal framework becomes a trap
chapters.bridge_from_prior: Slade's cease-and-desist notice has arrived at the site — Tayak reads it standing in the excavation trench.

chapters.act: Act II — early | Past timeline — Tessa's era
chapters.beat: 1743–1755: Tessa leads the ceremonies alone at twenty years old with no one to ask if she is doing it correctly; she makes the pipe bowls the way Matta taught her; she visits the mound regularly — not to dig but to remember, to walk the perimeter and recite the map in her head; her brother, who has converted to Christianity and taken a colonial name, tells her she is wasting her life; she tells him she is keeping it; they do not speak for three years.
chapters.title: Tessa Alone [Past — 1743–1755]
chapters.arc_point: Past: Tessa inherits the burden; her arc begins
chapters.bridge_from_prior: Matta has died — Tessa is now the sole keeper of the burial map and the ceremonial tradition; Nora continues the story to Tayak during the 48-hour wait.

chapters.beat: Wren discovers that the 1680s land grant that displaced the Piscataway settlement was issued to a family named Calvert — her own family; the land her great-great-grandmother's estate sits on was taken directly from the people whose mound Wren is now excavating; she sits in the university archive and does not move for twenty minutes; then she calls her mother; her mother says 'I know'; this is worse.
chapters.title: Wren's Discovery [Present — 2024]
chapters.arc_point: Reveal about secondary character's past changes relationships
chapters.bridge_from_prior: While Tayak deals with the legal crisis, Wren has continued researching the 1680s land grant she found in chapter 10 — she has now traced it forward.

chapters.act: Act II — early | Past timeline — Tessa's era
chapters.beat: 1762: Tessa's brother, now called Thomas, informs the colonial authorities that his sister is conducting 'heathen ceremonies' — not out of malice but out of genuine fear for her safety, believing conversion is the only protection available; the colonial constable visits Tessa's home; finds nothing; Tessa has moved everything to the mound; she does not report her brother; she does not forgive him either; she adds the shell gorget she has been making to the mound's third layer — a marker, a message, a record.
chapters.title: Tessa's Brother [Past — 1755–1762]
chapters.arc_point: Past: Tessa's moral complication — her brother's conversion and its consequences
chapters.bridge_from_prior: The estrangement between Tessa and her brother from chapter 27 has continued — it now reaches a crisis; Nora tells this part of the story to Tayak the following evening.

chapters.beat: Wren tells Tayak about the Calvert land grant; Tayak's first reaction is not sympathy — it is the cold recognition that Wren's family history is now a legal complication: if the Calvert estate's title chain is challenged, the dig becomes entangled in a property dispute that will bury the recognition petition; Tayak tells Wren to say nothing to anyone; Wren agrees; neither of them feels good about it.
chapters.title: Wren Tells Tayak [Present — 2024]
chapters.arc_point: Consequence of Wren's discovery reshapes team dynamic
chapters.bridge_from_prior: Wren has come directly from the archive to find Tayak — the Calvert discovery is the thread.

chapters.beat: Tayak submits the 1697 petition to the state — the voluntary surrender Marcus recommended; she does it without telling the tribal council first; she tells herself it is strategic; she knows it is also exhaustion; the document leaves her hands and she feels it go; she drives back to the mound and stands at the edge of the trench for a long time.
chapters.title: The Response [Present — 2024]
chapters.arc_point: Protagonist acts under pressure; moral cost paid
chapters.bridge_from_prior: The 48-hour deadline from Slade's notice is expiring — Tayak must respond.

chapters.act: Act II — early | Past timeline — Tessa's era
chapters.beat: 1762: Tessa places the shell gorget in the mound's third layer — below Matta's pipe bowl, below Okwi's oilskin; she has worn it at every ceremony she has led; it is the most personal thing she owns; she buries it because she has decided the mound is safer than any house, any body, any living memory; she speaks the names of the ancestors over it — all the names she knows, in order, going back as far as the names go; she adds her own name; she adds her brother's name, though he would not want her to.
chapters.title: The Shell Gorget [Past — 1762]
chapters.arc_point: Past: the artifact's burial — the moment that creates Stratum Three
chapters.bridge_from_prior: Tessa has added the shell gorget to the mound — this chapter dramatizes that act and its meaning.

chapters.beat: A shell gorget, pre-contact in style but 18th-century in manufacture — a deliberate archaism, someone making something old on purpose; Tayak photographs it and calls Nora; Nora says 'That's Tessa's — she made it herself'; Tayak asks how Nora knows; Nora says 'Because Tessa's granddaughter told her daughter, who told my grandmother Ida, who told me — the gorget is in the story'; Tayak understands for the first time that the oral history and the physical record are the same record.
chapters.title: Stratum Three: The Shell Gorget [Present — 2024]
chapters.arc_point: Fourth artifact; mound-as-vault confirmed; oral chain deepens
chapters.bridge_from_prior: The excavation has continued — the third stratum has been reached; the shell gorget is the find.

chapters.beat: Nora calls a private meeting with two of the oldest tribal members — women in their 70s and 80s who remember things; she tells them she is ready to speak about the mound; they tell her she should have spoken thirty years ago; she agrees; she begins to plan what she will say and to whom and in what order; she takes out the quilt and shows them the hidden panel for the first time.
chapters.title: The Elder Speaks [Present — 2024]
chapters.arc_point: Nora begins to move toward full disclosure
chapters.bridge_from_prior: Tayak's call from the trench has reached Nora — she described the gorget and Nora confirmed it.

chapters.beat: Voss submits a grant application to the National Science Foundation listing himself as principal investigator on the Charles County site — using Tayak's preliminary data without her knowledge or consent; Tayak finds out when a colleague forwards her the NSF portal listing; this is not ambiguous; this is theft; she prints the listing and drives to campus.
chapters.title: Voss Moves [Present — 2024]
chapters.arc_point: New dramatic problem: institutional betrayal
chapters.bridge_from_prior: The shell gorget has been photographed and logged — Voss has seen the preliminary report and is now acting on it.

chapters.act: Act II — middle | Past timeline — Ahanu's era
chapters.beat: circa 1205 CE: the third year of drought; Ahanu stands at the mound and counts the families who have left — seven in three years; Sokan stands beside her and says nothing, which is worse than anything he could say; the mound is the community's center of gravity — as long as people come to it, they have not entirely dispersed; Ahanu leads a ceremony; the rain does not come; the people come back the next day anyway.
chapters.title: Ahanu's Drought [Past — circa 1205 CE]
chapters.arc_point: Past: Ahanu's world established; the drought crisis begins
chapters.bridge_from_prior: Nora has told Tayak that the oral history goes back further than Tessa — that there are stories of a drought, a woman named Ahanu, and an older gorget; Tayak asks to hear them; Nora begins.

chapters.beat: Tayak confronts Voss; he does not deny it — he reframes it as 'protecting the project' from the political controversy Kimi's media campaign has created; he offers her co-investigator status; she tells him she will file a formal complaint with the university research office; he tells her, quietly, that doing so will trigger a review of her own permit, which was issued partly on the basis of her university affiliation; she leaves without answering.
chapters.title: The Confrontation [Present — 2024]
chapters.arc_point: Protagonist confronts institutional betrayal directly
chapters.bridge_from_prior: Tayak has printed the NSF listing and driven to campus — she is in Voss's office.

chapters.act: Act II — middle | Past timeline — Ahanu's era
chapters.beat: circa 1207 CE: Waya watches her father challenge Ahanu at the community gathering; he is right about the diagnosis — the community has drifted from the old ceremonies — and wrong about the cure, which is to shame the people who have drifted; Waya is the only person who can see both sides clearly and the only person who cannot say so without destroying her relationship with one of them; she says nothing; she hates herself for it.
chapters.title: Sokan and Waya [Past — circa 1205–1210 CE]
chapters.arc_point: Past: Sokan's challenge; Waya's position established
chapters.bridge_from_prior: Sokan's silence at the mound in chapter 36 has broken — he has now spoken publicly against Ahanu's leadership; Nora continues the story.

chapters.beat: Marcus, alone after the call, reviews the document he signed eighteen months ago: a memorandum of understanding with Chesapeake Heritage Development LLC, giving them right of first consultation on any tribal land designated for heritage tourism; he signed it to fund the recognition petition; if the mound becomes a protected site, the LLC has a contractual claim to its commercial development; he has told no one; he opens the document and reads it again, looking for a way out.
chapters.title: Marcus's Secret [Present — 2024]
chapters.arc_point: Reveal about Marcus's compromise — new dramatic problem
chapters.bridge_from_prior: Tayak has called Marcus from the parking lot outside Voss's building — she needs legal advice; Marcus's response is evasive in a way she notices.

chapters.act: Act II — middle | Past timeline — Ahanu's era
chapters.beat: circa 1210 CE: the rain comes — not because of the ceremony, and Ahanu is honest enough to know that — but the ceremony held the people together long enough for the rain to matter; Sokan comes to her the morning after the first real rain in three years and gives her the shell gorget he has carved — a gesture of reconciliation that costs him more than she will ever know; she accepts it; she does not say she forgives him; she wears it; this is the same gesture.
chapters.title: Ahanu and the Rain [Past — circa 1210 CE]
chapters.arc_point: Past: the drought breaks; Sokan's reconciliation; the gorget's origin
chapters.bridge_from_prior: The community crisis from chapters 36 and 38 has reached its peak — this chapter resolves it.

chapters.beat: A second shell gorget, genuinely pre-contact, circa 1200 CE; Tayak photographs it and calls Nora; Nora says 'That one is older than Tessa — that goes back to Ahanu, and before her'; Tayak asks how the story reaches that far; Nora says 'Because Ahanu's granddaughter carried it forward, and it came down through the women — Ida told me the whole chain'; Tayak asks Nora to tell her the chain from the beginning; Nora says 'Not yet — go deeper first.'
chapters.title: Stratum Four: The Shell Gorget (Older) [Present — 2024]
chapters.arc_point: Fifth artifact; oral chain extends further back; Tayak's personal connection begins to form
chapters.bridge_from_prior: The excavation has continued — the fourth stratum has been reached; a second, older shell gorget is the find.

chapters.beat: Kimi discovers that Chesapeake Heritage Development LLC is a subsidiary of the same real estate group behind the highway expansion — meaning the company that threatened the mound is now positioned to profit from its protection; she does not yet know Marcus signed an MOU with them; she calls Tayak with the information; Tayak is quiet for a long time; then she says 'Send me everything you have.'
chapters.title: Kimi Investigates [Present — 2024]
chapters.arc_point: Kimi's campaign produces unexpected intelligence
chapters.bridge_from_prior: Kimi, trying to make amends for the Post disaster, has been doing her own research — she has found a thread connecting Chesapeake Heritage Development to the highway expansion.

chapters.act: Act II — middle | Past timeline — Ahanu's era
chapters.beat: circa 1212 CE: Waya's third child, a daughter, dies in her second year — a fever, quick and total; Waya does not speak of it to anyone; she hunts alone for three days; when she returns, Ahanu gives her the shell gorget — the one Sokan gave Ahanu — and says 'Wear it until you are ready to give it to someone else'; Waya wears it for twenty years; when she finally gives it away, it is to her oldest daughter, with instructions to add it to the mound when the time comes.
chapters.title: Waya's Grief [Past — circa 1212 CE]
chapters.arc_point: Past: Waya's private loss; the copper pendant's transmission in this era
chapters.bridge_from_prior: The reconciliation between Ahanu and Sokan in chapter 40 has eased the community's tension — but Waya's private grief has not been addressed; Nora tells this part of the story.

chapters.beat: The hearing goes badly for Tayak in the way institutional hearings always go badly for the person without institutional power: Voss's grant application is ruled an 'administrative error,' he is asked to amend it, and Tayak is advised to 'consider the optics' of pursuing the matter further given the 'political sensitivity' of the site; she is not fired; she is warned; the distinction is thin; she drives back to the mound and digs for four hours without stopping.
chapters.title: The University Hearing [Present — 2024]
chapters.arc_point: Institutional crisis peaks
chapters.bridge_from_prior: Tayak filed the complaint against Voss — the university research office has convened a hearing; this is it.

chapters.beat: A copper pendant, Hopewell-influenced, circa 200–300 CE; Tayak photographs it and calls Nora; Nora is silent for a long moment and then says 'That is the oldest thing in the story — that pendant goes back further than I can tell you tonight; come to the house tomorrow; I need to tell you the whole chain from the beginning, and I need to do it in person.'
chapters.title: Stratum Five: The Copper Pendant [Present — 2024]
chapters.arc_point: Sixth artifact; the chain of oral tradition approaches its deepest link
chapters.bridge_from_prior: The excavation has continued — the fifth stratum has been reached; the copper pendant is the find.

chapters.act: Act II — middle | Past timeline — the pendant's era
chapters.beat: circa 200–300 CE: the pendant came to Waya's ancestor through a Hopewell trading network — a gift from a trader who passed through once and was never seen again; it has been in the family for four generations by the time Waya wears it; she gives it to her daughter with the same words her mother used: 'This came from far away — it means we are not alone'; her daughter wears it for thirty years; when she dies, she asks that it be buried with the mound's other objects — not lost, but kept.
chapters.title: The Pendant Passes [Past — circa 200–300 CE]
chapters.arc_point: Past: the copper pendant's journey through generations — the chain of transmission
chapters.bridge_from_prior: The copper pendant Tayak found in Stratum Five — Nora has begun telling its story; this chapter dramatizes the pendant's transmission.

chapters.beat: Wren's mother calls to say the family has been contacted by a Maryland property attorney asking about the Calvert land grant — someone has been researching the title chain; Wren realizes Kimi's research has gotten close to the Calvert connection; she must choose: tell Tayak that the title chain is about to become public, which will help the recognition case but expose the secret Tayak asked her to keep — or stay silent and let it surface on its own terms; she sits with this for one day; then she calls Tayak.
chapters.title: Wren's Choice [Present — 2024]
chapters.arc_point: Secondary character faces her own moral complication
chapters.bridge_from_prior: The university hearing's outcome has reached Wren — she was not called to testify, though she could have been.

chapters.act: Act II — middle | Past timeline — the pendant's era
chapters.beat: circa 300 CE: Waya's daughter places the copper pendant in the mound's fifth layer — below the shell gorget, below the antler figure, below the pipe bowl, below the oilskin; she speaks the names of everyone who has worn it; she adds the name of the trader who brought it, though she does not know his name — she says 'the one who came from far away' and this is enough; she covers the pendant with earth and goes home; the mound is now five layers deep.
chapters.title: The Pendant Buried [Past — circa 300 CE]
chapters.arc_point: Past: the artifact's burial — the moment that creates Stratum Five
chapters.bridge_from_prior: The pendant's transmission from chapter 46 has reached its end — the burial is the act that creates the archaeological record.

chapters.beat: Wren tells Tayak everything: the Calvert title chain, the attorney inquiry, and the fact that she has already sent the land grant documentation to Marcus's legal team without asking Tayak first; Tayak is furious and then, slowly, not — because the documentation is exactly what the recognition petition needs; the right thing happened for the wrong reasons; Tayak does not know how to feel about this; she tells Wren: 'Come back to the site — we're going deeper.'
chapters.title: Wren Speaks [Present — 2024]
chapters.arc_point: Consequence of earlier choice becomes inevitable
chapters.bridge_from_prior: Wren has decided — she calls Tayak; this chapter is Tayak receiving that call.

chapters.beat: Kimi, having connected the Chesapeake Heritage Development thread, confronts Marcus directly at the tribal council office; she has the MOU — found through a public records request she filed three weeks ago and forgot about; Marcus does not deny it; two council members are present; the room goes very quiet; Kimi does not say anything else; she does not need to.
chapters.title: Marcus Exposed [Present — 2024]
chapters.arc_point: Midpoint reversal: ally becomes obstacle
chapters.bridge_from_prior: Wren's land grant documentation has arrived at Marcus's office — and with it, Kimi's research on Chesapeake Heritage Development; Marcus now knows both pieces are in play.

chapters.beat: An emergency tribal council meeting: Marcus offers to resign; half the council wants him to; the other half argues that losing him now, with the recognition petition at a critical stage, is worse than the compromise he made; Tayak, who has no vote but is asked to speak, says the one thing she knows to be true: the mound is the argument, not Marcus, and they need to let her finish the dig.
chapters.title: The Council Fractures [Present — 2024]
chapters.arc_point: Political foundation of the recognition fight cracks
chapters.bridge_from_prior: Kimi has called Tayak immediately after the confrontation with Marcus — Tayak arrives at the council office.

chapters.act: Act II — late | Past timeline — Kessik's era
chapters.beat: circa 500 CE: Kessik has traveled north and seen the great mounds; she has understood something about them that she cannot yet articulate — they are not graves, they are arguments; they say: we were here, we are here, we will be here; she comes home and tells her community she wants to build one; her brother Pell says 'To what end?'; she says 'To every end'; he does not understand; he will.
chapters.title: Kessik's Vision [Past — circa 500 CE]
chapters.arc_point: Past: Kessik's world established; the mound-building project begins
chapters.bridge_from_prior: Nora, continuing the oral chain to Tayak, now reaches the story of Kessik — the woman who built the mound's earliest deliberate structure.

chapters.beat: Slade drives to the county records office and pulls his own family's title chain; the gap he has always suspected is there: a 1683 land transfer from a 'Piscataway settlement' to a colonial grantee, with no record of consent or compensation; his family's farm — two miles from the mound — sits on the same dispossession; he drives home and does not tell his daughter, who is a tribal rights attorney; he sits in his car in the driveway for twenty minutes.
chapters.title: Slade's Family [Present — 2024]
chapters.arc_point: Antagonist's private world intersects with the plot
chapters.bridge_from_prior: The Calvert land grant research, now circulating through Marcus's legal team, has reached Slade's office — Slade has seen the 1680s grant and recognized the county.

chapters.act: Act II — late | Past timeline — Kessik's era
chapters.beat: circa 507 CE: Pell watches his sister lead the first community meeting about the mound; he watches the old people's faces — the ones who remember the stories of the northern mounds, who have been waiting for someone to say this; he does not change his mind that day; he changes it three days later, alone, thinking about what it would mean for his children to stand on something their grandparents built; he goes to Kessik and says 'Tell me where to start.'
chapters.title: Pell Converts [Past — circa 505–510 CE]
chapters.arc_point: Past: Pell's skepticism breaks; the mound project gains momentum
chapters.bridge_from_prior: Kessik's proposal from chapter 52 has been met with community skepticism — Pell is the loudest skeptic.

chapters.beat: A carved antler figure, circa 500 CE; Tayak photographs it and calls Nora; Nora says 'That's from before the mound was the mound — that's from when it was being built'; Tayak asks who built it; Nora says 'A woman named Kessik — and her brother Pell who didn't believe her at first'; Tayak looks at the figure in her hand and understands: this is not a burial site; this is a library; and someone has been reading it aloud for two thousand years.
chapters.title: Stratum Six: The Antler Figure [Present — 2024]
chapters.arc_point: Seventh artifact; Tayak begins to understand the full scope of the chain
chapters.bridge_from_prior: The council crisis has been temporarily stabilized — Tayak is back at the mound, which is the only place the political chaos cannot follow her.

chapters.act: Act II — late | Past timeline — Kessik's era
chapters.beat: circa 510–525 CE: the mound takes fifteen years to build; Kessik is ill for the last three of them — a slow decline she refuses to acknowledge publicly; Pell builds the final layer; when it is finished, Kessik walks to the top and stands there for a long time; she says 'Now it will remember us'; Pell says 'You built it'; she says 'We built it — that's the point'; she places the antler figure in the mound's sixth layer; she dies the following winter.
chapters.title: The Mound Rises [Past — circa 510–525 CE]
chapters.arc_point: Past: the mound's construction — the founding act of the tradition
chapters.bridge_from_prior: Pell's conversion from chapter 54 has given the project momentum — the building begins.

chapters.beat: Kimi holds a press conference outside the mound site; she reads from the 1697 petition — now in state custody but a public document — and names the Calvert land grant; three television cameras, a dozen reporters; Slade watches it on his office computer; Voss watches it on his phone; Tayak, standing behind Kimi, says nothing and is photographed saying nothing, which is its own statement.
chapters.title: The Press Conference [Present — 2024]
chapters.arc_point: New dramatic problem: public battle forces Tayak's hand
chapters.bridge_from_prior: Kimi, energized by the Marcus confrontation and the council's fractured response, has organized a press conference — she told Tayak; Tayak said 'not yet'; Kimi did it anyway.

chapters.act: Act II — late | Past timeline — Kessik's era
chapters.beat: circa 526 CE: Pell stands at the mound the morning after Kessik's burial — she is in the earth now, not in the mound but near it, as she asked; he understands for the first time what she meant: the mound is not for the dead; it is for the living who come after; he tells his children this; he tells his grandchildren; he tells everyone who will listen; he is not a storyteller — he is an engineer — but this one story he tells correctly, every time, for the rest of his life.
chapters.title: Pell's Grief [Past — circa 526 CE]
chapters.arc_point: Past: Pell's arc closes; the mound's meaning crystallizes
chapters.bridge_from_prior: Kessik's death from chapter 56 — Pell is now alone with what they built.

chapters.beat: The state announces it is fast-tracking a heritage designation for the mound — not as a tribal site, but as a 'colonial-era historical landmark,' which would place it under state management and effectively end the tribal recognition petition's land-based argument; Tayak has thirty days to produce counter-evidence or the designation stands; she calls Marcus; she calls Nora; she goes back to the mound.
chapters.title: The State Responds [Present — 2024]
chapters.arc_point: Antagonist escalates; recognition petition threatened
chapters.bridge_from_prior: The press conference has triggered a formal response from the Maryland Governor's office — Slade delivers it to Tayak in person.

chapters.beat: Nora calls Marcus and tells him she is ready to give a formal affidavit; she tells him what she knows: the mound's deepest chamber contains the remains of the woman who founded their family's line on this land — a woman whose name is in the oral history Ida passed to her, whose name connects to the 1697 petition, and whose identity Nora can trace through four generations of told stories; Marcus listens; when she finishes, he says 'Why didn't you tell us thirty years ago?'; she says 'Because thirty years ago, no one was listening.'
chapters.title: Nora's Decision [Present — 2024]
chapters.arc_point: Nora commits to full disclosure
chapters.bridge_from_prior: Nora has seen the press conference on television — she saw Tayak's face behind Kimi, and she recognized the expression.

chapters.act: Act II — late | Past timeline — the founding era
chapters.beat: circa 100 BC: Yanu's community lives on the Potomac watershed — a good life, a full life, a life with no knowledge of what will come; Yanu is known for reading weather from birds; she has four living children and one dead one — a daughter, Taya, who died in her second year; the copper pendant around Yanu's neck was made for Taya by a Hopewell trader who passed through once; Yanu has worn it every day since Taya died; she does not know what to do with the grief; she has not yet found the answer.
chapters.title: Yanu's World [Past — circa 100 BC]
chapters.arc_point: Past: the founding ancestor's world established; the deepest timeline begins
chapters.bridge_from_prior: Nora has now told Tayak that the oral chain goes all the way back to a woman named Yanu — the woman at the bottom of everything; this chapter dramatizes Yanu's world.

chapters.beat: Tayak sits with Nora while a tribal attorney records the affidavit; Nora speaks for two hours; she names every generation she knows, traces the oral history of the mound, and describes the quilt's hidden map; Tayak listens to things she has never heard; some of them make her angry; some of them make her understand things she has spent her career not understanding; at the end, Nora says 'Now go find her.'
chapters.title: The Affidavit [Present — 2024]
chapters.arc_point: Oral history enters the legal record
chapters.bridge_from_prior: Marcus has called Tayak immediately after Nora's call — Tayak drives to her grandmother's house.

chapters.act: Act II — late | Past timeline — the founding era
chapters.beat: circa 100 BC: Taya is born in the spring — a quiet child, watchful, with her mother's gift for reading birds; she dies in her second winter — a fever, quick and total; Yanu holds her for a long time after; Ranu tries to speak and cannot; the community gathers; Yanu does not want the community; she wants her daughter; she takes the copper pendant from her own neck and holds it; she does not know yet what she will do with it; she knows she cannot keep it and she cannot give it away.
chapters.title: Taya [Past — circa 100 BC]
chapters.arc_point: Past: Taya's life and death — the event that creates the founding burial
chapters.bridge_from_prior: Yanu's world from chapter 61 — the death of Taya is the event that sets everything in motion.

chapters.beat: Voss withdraws his NSF application and offers Tayak a formal letter of institutional support for the tribal recognition petition — he does this because his daughter called him after seeing the press conference and told him he was on the wrong side; Tayak accepts the support; she does not forgive him; she notes the distinction in her field log; she goes back to the mound.
chapters.title: Voss Recants [Present — 2024]
chapters.arc_point: Institutional obstacle partially removed — but at a cost
chapters.bridge_from_prior: The press conference and the state's colonial landmark announcement have reached Voss — he has done the political calculation and called Tayak.

chapters.act: Act II — late | Past timeline — the founding era
chapters.beat: circa 99 BC: Ranu tries three times to tell Taya's story at the community gathering; each time he stops — the words are wrong, too large, too performed, too much like the stories he tells about other people's lives; Taya was not a story; she was his daughter; he goes home and carves a small figure from antler — simpler than anything he has made before, just a shape that means 'child'; he gives it to Yanu; she holds it and says 'I know what to do'; he does not ask what she means; he trusts her; this is the most important thing he has ever done.
chapters.title: Ranu Tries to Tell the Story [Past — circa 99 BC]
chapters.arc_point: Past: Ranu's arc; the failure of public grief; Yanu's private solution takes shape
chapters.bridge_from_prior: Taya's death from chapter 63 — Ranu is the community's storyteller and cannot tell this story.

chapters.beat: Elena tells her father she has been offered a position with the Piscataway tribal legal team; she asks him if she should take it; he tells her to do what she thinks is right; she tells him she already has; the call ends; Slade looks at the colonial landmark designation paperwork on his desk and does not sign it.
chapters.title: Slade's Daughter [Present — 2024]
chapters.arc_point: Antagonist's private world collides with his public role
chapters.bridge_from_prior: Slade's daughter Elena — a tribal rights attorney — has seen the press conference; she calls her father.

chapters.act: Act II — late | Past timeline — the founding era
chapters.beat: circa 99 BC: Yanu carries the copper pendant to the place where the earth rises slightly — the place that will become the mound, though it is not yet a mound, just a rise her community has always treated as significant without knowing why; she digs with her hands; she places the pendant in the earth; she places Ranu's carved figure beside it; she says Taya's name; she says it again; she says it a third time, so the earth will know it; she covers the pendant with soil and sits beside it until the sun goes down; she does not know she has started something; she is only trying to keep her daughter's name alive.
chapters.title: Yanu Goes to the Earth [Past — circa 99 BC]
chapters.arc_point: Past: the founding act — Yanu buries the pendant; the mound's deepest layer is created
chapters.bridge_from_prior: Ranu's gift of the antler figure in chapter 65 has given Yanu the clarity she needed — this chapter is the founding act.

chapters.beat: Marcus calls a full tribal council meeting and discloses the MOU publicly; he does not resign; he presents the legal argument for voiding it and asks the council to vote on whether to pursue it; the vote is close; it passes; he has survived — barely — and the cost is that everyone now knows exactly what he did and why; he drives home and coaches lacrosse practice and does not think about it for two hours; this is the best he can do.
chapters.title: Marcus Stays [Present — 2024]
chapters.arc_point: Marcus's arc: he chooses the tribe over self-protection
chapters.bridge_from_prior: Elena Slade has joined the tribal legal team — Marcus has met with her; she has told him the MOU with Chesapeake Heritage Development is voidable.

chapters.act: Act III — early | Past timeline — the founding era
chapters.beat: circa 98–80 BC: other people begin to bring things to the rise in the earth — a woman whose son died, a man whose wife died — they do not ask Yanu's permission, they simply come, as if the place has always been for this; one day a young woman asks 'What do you say when you put something in the earth?'; Yanu says 'You say the name'; the young woman says 'Just the name?'; Yanu says 'The name is everything'; this is the ceremony; this is all the ceremony there has ever been.
chapters.title: Yanu After [Past — circa 98–80 BC]
chapters.arc_point: Past: Yanu's life after the burial; the tradition begins without her knowing it
chapters.bridge_from_prior: The founding act from chapter 67 — Yanu's life continues; the consequences of the burial unfold.

chapters.beat: Tayak calls the full team back to the site and announces they are going to the deepest layer; she tells them what Nora said; she tells them what she expects to find; she does not yet tell them the personal connection — she is not certain of it herself; she tells them 'We have twenty-two days'; Wren looks at her and says 'We'll be ready'; Tayak believes her.
chapters.title: The Thirty-Day Clock [Present — 2024]
chapters.arc_point: Deadline pressure forces final excavation push
chapters.bridge_from_prior: The council vote has given Marcus a mandate — he calls Tayak and tells her she has institutional and legal support; she needs to produce the physical evidence before the thirty days expire.

chapters.act: Act III — early | Past timeline — the founding era
chapters.beat: circa 80 BC: Ranu tells Taya's story at the community gathering — he has been preparing for twenty years; he tells it simply, no embellishment, no performance, just the facts: a child was born, she died, her mother put her name in the earth, and now the earth keeps it; the community is very still; when he finishes, an old man says 'Tell it again'; he does; this is the first time the story has been told; it will be told for two thousand years.
chapters.title: Ranu's Story [Past — circa 80 BC]
chapters.arc_point: Past: Ranu finally tells Taya's story; the founding act enters the community's memory
chapters.bridge_from_prior: The tradition Yanu started in chapter 69 has grown — Ranu has been watching it; he is finally ready to tell the story.

chapters.beat: Wren meets with the Calvert family attorney and tells him she will not contest the land grant research and will provide her own documentation to the tribal legal team; her mother calls her a fool; Wren tells her mother she has been a fool for twenty-eight years and is trying to stop; she goes back to the trench; she draws every artifact she has found, by hand, in her field notebook; it takes her all night.
chapters.title: Wren's Restitution [Present — 2024]
chapters.arc_point: Secondary character resolves her moral complication
chapters.bridge_from_prior: The final excavation push has begun — Wren is on site, and the Calvert family attorney has now formally contacted her.

chapters.beat: The deepest chamber opens: inside, a burial, intact, with grave goods — copper, shell, ochre — and a carved wooden figure that matches the figure in Nora's quilt exactly; Tayak does not touch anything yet; she photographs everything; then she picks up the wooden figure and reads the carving on its base — a name, incised in a notation system she has seen in one other place: the quilt's hidden panel; she does not understand it yet; she calls Nora.
chapters.title: Stratum Seven: The Deepest Layer [Present — 2024]
chapters.arc_point: The central discovery — the climax of the excavation
chapters.bridge_from_prior: The team has been excavating for six days since chapter 70 — they have reached the final chamber.

chapters.beat: Nora begins to cry — the first time Tayak has ever heard her grandmother cry; Nora says the figure's name: Taya; and then: Yanu, the woman who buried her; and then, quietly, the thing she has been holding for sixty years: 'Tayak — your name is not a coincidence; it grew from Taya's name, passed down and changed and kept for two thousand years; you have been excavating your own family's grave'; Tayak sits in the earth her ancestor was buried in and does not speak for a long time.
chapters.title: The Name [Present — 2024]
chapters.arc_point: Personal revelation crystallizes the dramatic question — the deferred revelation lands
chapters.bridge_from_prior: Tayak has called Nora from inside the chamber — she is describing the wooden figure and the carved notation.

chapters.act: Act III — early | Past timeline — the founding era
chapters.beat: circa 60 BC: Yanu is old; her oldest daughter has a daughter, and that daughter has been given the name Taya — the first time the name has been used again; Yanu holds the child and says 'You are named for someone who was here before you — she is still here; she is in the earth'; the child does not understand; she will; Yanu dies the following spring, buried near the mound, not in it — she never asked to be in it; the mound was for Taya; it was always for Taya.
chapters.title: Yanu's Name Lives [Past — circa 60 BC]
chapters.arc_point: Past: the name passes forward — the chain of naming that reaches Tayak
chapters.bridge_from_prior: Ranu's story from chapter 71 has entered the community's memory — Yanu is now old; this is her final chapter.

chapters.beat: Tayak must decide what to put in the official report: the scientific evidence is overwhelming, but to make the personal connection explicit — that this is her direct ancestor — will expose her to the charge of bias that will let Slade and Voss dismiss everything; she can write a clean scientific report that protects the evidence but erases herself from the story, or she can write the full truth and risk the whole case; she writes the full truth; she writes it in one sitting, without stopping, and does not reread it before she sends it.
chapters.title: The Decision [Present — 2024]
chapters.arc_point: Protagonist's central moral crisis — the climax of her arc
chapters.bridge_from_prior: The discovery from chapters 73–74 must now be reported — Tayak is writing the field report.

chapters.beat: Slade reads Tayak's report for three hours; he reads the 1697 petition, the oral history affidavit, the artifact chain, and the personal disclosure; he thinks about his own family's title gap; he thinks about Elena; he picks up the phone and calls the Governor's office; he tells them he cannot recommend the colonial landmark designation; he does not say why; he does not need to.
chapters.title: Slade Reads the Report [Present — 2024]
chapters.arc_point: Antagonist confronts the evidence
chapters.bridge_from_prior: Tayak's report has been submitted to the state preservation office — Slade is reading it.

chapters.beat: Voss tells Tayak the report is the most important piece of Chesapeake archaeology in fifty years; he also tells her the personal disclosure will be used against her; she tells him she knows; he asks if she wants him to help her remove it; she says no; he says he will support it anyway; she thanks him — the first time she has thanked him for anything — and hangs up.
chapters.title: Voss Reads the Report [Present — 2024]
chapters.arc_point: Institutional establishment confronts the evidence
chapters.bridge_from_prior: The report has been simultaneously submitted to the university — Voss has called Tayak.

chapters.beat: Kimi spends forty-eight hours building a digital archive: the report, the 1697 petition, Nora's affidavit, the artifact photographs, the land grant chain, and a video of Nora speaking the names of the ancestors — the full oral chain, from Yanu to Taya to every name in between, ending with Tayak; she publishes it all at once; by morning it has been shared 200,000 times; the Governor's office issues a statement saying the colonial landmark designation is 'under review.'
chapters.title: Kimi's Archive [Present — 2024]
chapters.arc_point: Kimi's campaign becomes the public record
chapters.bridge_from_prior: Tayak has sent Kimi the report — with permission to use it publicly, which is the first time Tayak has given Kimi explicit authorization.

chapters.beat: Tayak testifies before the Maryland Heritage Commission; she presents the scientific evidence; then she presents the oral history evidence — the chain of told stories, each link a named person who told the next, going back two thousand years — and she describes it not as folklore but as a form of record-keeping that Western science has always dismissed and that this mound has just corroborated artifact by artifact; the room is very quiet; Slade, sitting on the commission panel, does not ask a single hostile question.
chapters.title: The Hearing [Present — 2024]
chapters.arc_point: Legal and political climax approaches
chapters.bridge_from_prior: The public response to Kimi's archive has forced a formal state hearing — Tayak has been called to testify.

chapters.beat: Nora testifies for forty minutes; she names every generation she knows; she describes the quilt; she brings the quilt and unrolls it on the commission table — the stitched map of the mound's interior, made by a woman who learned it from a woman who learned it from a woman; the commission chair asks how old the pattern is; Nora says 'As old as the mound'; the room does not recover from this.
chapters.title: Nora Testifies [Present — 2024]
chapters.arc_point: Oral tradition enters the formal record
chapters.bridge_from_prior: After Tayak's testimony, the commission has called Nora — she is the affidavit's author and they want her in person.

chapters.beat: Elena tells her father she is proud of him for not signing the colonial landmark designation; he tells her he is not sure he deserves that; she tells him what she knows about the Calvert title chain and what it means for their own family's land; he asks what she thinks they should do; she says 'Whatever the tribe asks'; he nods; this is the most important conversation of his life and it takes four minutes.
chapters.title: Elena Slade [Present — 2024]
chapters.arc_point: Antagonist's arc resolves through his daughter
chapters.bridge_from_prior: The hearing has recessed — Slade has stepped into the hallway and found Elena waiting for him.

chapters.beat: Marcus negotiates the voiding of the Chesapeake Heritage Development MOU in exchange for the tribe's agreement not to pursue a public lawsuit over the colonial land grants — a compromise that costs the tribe a potential financial settlement but preserves the recognition petition's momentum; he presents it to the council; this time the vote is not close.
chapters.title: Marcus's Redemption [Present — 2024]
chapters.arc_point: Marcus's arc resolves
chapters.bridge_from_prior: The hearing has produced a groundswell — Marcus has been in back-channel negotiations with the Governor's office since Kimi's archive went viral.

chapters.beat: The Maryland Heritage Commission rules that the Charles County mound is a site of continuous Indigenous cultural significance and recommends its designation as a tribally controlled heritage site; the colonial landmark designation is withdrawn; the ruling formally acknowledges the Piscataway's unbroken presence on this land — from Yanu's first burial in 100 BC to Tayak's trowel in 2024 — and recommends the recognition petition be fast-tracked; Tayak hears the ruling and feels nothing for a moment; then she feels everything.
chapters.title: The Commission Rules [Present — 2024]
chapters.arc_point: Central dramatic question answered
chapters.bridge_from_prior: The commission has deliberated for six days since the hearing — Tayak is in the hearing room for the ruling.

chapters.act: Act III — climax aftermath | Present timeline
chapters.beat: Tayak stands outside the commission building and understands what she has done: she has won the argument and surrendered her scientific neutrality permanently; she will never be the objective researcher again; she is now, in the record, a descendant testifying about her own ancestors; she decides this is not a loss; it takes her the length of a cigarette — she doesn't smoke — to decide it; she calls Nora; Nora answers on the first ring and says 'I know — I heard'; Tayak says 'We won'; Nora says 'We always knew.'
chapters.title: What It Costs Tayak [Present — 2024]
chapters.arc_point: Protagonist's emotional reckoning
chapters.bridge_from_prior: The ruling has just been delivered — Tayak steps outside the hearing room.

chapters.act: Act III — climax aftermath | Present timeline
chapters.beat: Slade calls his brother, who manages the family farm; he tells him they need to talk about the land; his brother asks what kind of talk; Slade says 'The kind where we find out what's right and do it'; his brother is silent for a long time; then he says 'Elena put you up to this'; Slade says 'Yes'; this is the most honest thing he has said in years.
chapters.title: What It Costs Slade [Present — 2024]
chapters.arc_point: Antagonist's reckoning
chapters.bridge_from_prior: Slade was in the hearing room for the ruling — he voted in favor; he is now in his car in the parking garage.

chapters.act: Act III — climax aftermath | Present timeline
chapters.beat: Nora watches the news coverage and sees her own face — the quilt on the commission table — and understands that she has finally done the thing she should have done thirty years ago, and that the thirty years are gone; she does not regret speaking; she regrets the silence that preceded it; she goes to her sewing room and begins a new quilt panel: the mound, open, with light coming out of it; she works until midnight; she is not tired.
chapters.title: What It Costs Nora [Present — 2024]
chapters.arc_point: Secondary character's reckoning — the secret's full cost
chapters.bridge_from_prior: Tayak has called Nora from outside the commission building — Nora is at home, watching the news.

chapters.beat: Kimi adds the commission ruling to the digital archive and posts a final video: not a call to action, just Nora's voice reading the names of the ancestors — the full oral chain, from Yanu to Taya to every name in between — over photographs of the artifacts; it is the most-watched thing she has ever made; she watches the view counter climb and feels, for the first time, that she has done something that will last; she calls her boyfriend and tells him about it; he says 'Tell me the names'; she does.
chapters.title: Kimi's Archive, Continued [Present — 2024]
chapters.arc_point: Public record secured
chapters.bridge_from_prior: The ruling has been announced — Kimi has been watching the live stream from DC.

chapters.beat: Wren submits the complete field documentation — 847 pages, every artifact illustrated by hand, every stratum mapped in three dimensions; she lists Tayak as principal investigator and herself as field assistant; she adds a personal note in the acknowledgments section that names the Calvert land grant and her family's connection to it; her mother does not speak to her for a month; Wren considers this a reasonable price.
chapters.title: Wren's Report [Present — 2024]
chapters.arc_point: Scientific record secured; Wren's arc closes
chapters.bridge_from_prior: The ruling has been made — Wren is at the university, completing the final field documentation.

chapters.beat: Tayak oversees the careful resealing of the deepest chamber; the wooden figure is returned to the earth; the copper pendant is returned; the shell gorgets are returned; the pipe bowl is returned; the antler figure is returned; each artifact goes back to the layer where it was found; Tayak places her hand on the closed earth and says the name — Taya — out loud, for the first time, to the ground; then she says Yanu; then she says all the names she knows, in order; Wren is there; neither of them speaks afterward for a long time.
chapters.title: The Mound, Closed [Present — 2024]
chapters.arc_point: The physical site is returned
chapters.bridge_from_prior: The documentation is complete — the tribe has voted to close the deepest chamber and seal it under tribal authority.

chapters.beat: Marcus submits the petition package to the BIA — 1,400 pages, including the commission ruling, Nora's affidavit, Tayak's report, and Wren's field documentation; the BIA officer tells him it will take eighteen months to two years to process; Marcus says 'We've been waiting since 1697 — we can wait two more years'; he means it; he also books a flight home and sleeps on the plane for the first time in months.
chapters.title: The Federal Petition [Present — 2024]
chapters.arc_point: Recognition fight continues — the larger battle is not over
chapters.bridge_from_prior: The state ruling has been formally submitted to the Bureau of Indian Affairs as supporting evidence for the federal recognition petition — Marcus is in Washington.

chapters.beat: Voss's foreword is generous, accurate, and gives Tayak full credit; it also, in its final paragraph, quietly revises the central argument of his own famous monograph on Chesapeake pre-contact trade networks, citing Tayak's findings; it is the closest he will ever come to an apology; Tayak reads it twice and decides it is enough.
chapters.title: Voss's Footnote [Present — 2024]
chapters.arc_point: Institutional world adjusts
chapters.bridge_from_prior: Tayak has received the published version of the field report — Voss has written a foreword.

chapters.beat: Nora finishes the quilt; the final panel shows the mound from above, closed and green, with a figure standing beside it — a woman, small, with a trowel; Nora gives the quilt to Tayak and tells her 'Your great-great-grandmother's grandmother made the first panel; I made the last; you're in the middle'; Tayak hangs it in her office at the university, where it is the first thing students see when they walk in.
chapters.title: Nora's Quilt, Finished [Present — 2024]
chapters.arc_point: Nora's arc closes
chapters.bridge_from_prior: Tayak has visited Nora after reading Voss's foreword — she has brought a copy of the published report.

chapters.beat: The mound site has been fenced, signed, and opened to tribal members for the first time; children from the tribal school walk the perimeter; an elder leads a ceremony; Tayak stands at the edge and watches and does not excavate anything; she is, for the first time in her professional life, simply present on the land without a trowel in her hand; she finds she does not miss it; a child asks her what is in the mound; she says 'Names'; the child says 'Whose names?'; she says 'Yours.'
chapters.title: The Site, One Year Later [Present — 2025]
chapters.arc_point: The world of the novel settles
chapters.bridge_from_prior: One year has passed since the commission ruling — Tayak is at the mound site for the first tribal heritage day.

chapters.beat: The same voice from the prologue speaks again — but now we know whose voice it is; Yanu is still there, in the dark, surrounded by the things her descendants returned to her: the pendant, the figures, the gorgets, the pipe bowl, the oilskin; above her, the ground is green; above the ground, a woman with a trowel she is not using stands in the sun and says a name; the name is Taya; it is also Tayak; it is also every name in between; the ground keeps them; the ground has always kept them; they were never lost; they were waiting — and the story of how they were found was told, as it had always been told, by one person to the next, in the dark, out loud, so the earth would know it.
chapters.title: Epilogue: What the Ground Keeps
chapters.arc_point: Resolution and echo of the prologue — both timelines converge
chapters.bridge_from_prior: The heritage day from chapter 94 — the mound is now protected; the epilogue returns to the ancestral voice of the prologue and completes the circle.

characters.name: Dr. Tayak Moyaone
characters.archetype: The scientist-warrior: a credentialed archaeologist who uses academic tools as weapons in a political fight for her people's survival.
characters.description: Piscataway Nation member, late 30s, assistant professor at University of Maryland. Grew up in La Plata, Charles County, raised by her grandmother Nora after her parents' deaths. Collects vintage topographic maps as a hobby. Has a close non-plot friendship with her colleague Dr. Priya Suresh, a South Asian-American geologist, with whom she argues about cricket and eats terrible campus food. Private worry: she has begun to suspect her grandmother knew exactly what was in that mound and never told her.
characters.terrified_by: Reaching the deepest layer and finding proof that her grandmother deliberately concealed the mound's significance from her, meaning Tayak's entire career has been built on a lie of omission.
characters.humiliated_by: Being dismissed as an advocate rather than a scientist — having her findings attributed to bias rather than evidence.
characters.made_happy_by: Standing inside a completed, protected, tribally controlled heritage site and knowing her name is on the report that made it happen.
characters.dramatic_question: Will Tayak sacrifice her scientific reputation and personal boundaries to testify that the mound is her family's sacred ground, knowing that doing so may win the tribe's recognition but end her career?
characters.off_axis_attribute: She is meticulous and fearless in the field but is privately terrified of her own emotional responses to the work — she has trained herself to feel nothing at the trowel's edge, because she knows that feeling something would destroy her scientific credibility, and she suspects it would confirm what her colleagues already whisper: that she is too close to the material to be objective.

characters.name: Nora Moyaone
characters.role: Secondary POV character; Tayak's grandmother and the keeper of oral tradition
characters.archetype: The elder who holds the secret — not a wise mentor who dispenses answers, but a frightened old woman who has spent sixty years deciding whether to speak.
characters.description: 82 years old, lives in the same La Plata house where she raised Tayak. Former schoolteacher. Makes elaborate quilts using patterns she says came from her own grandmother. Attends every tribal council meeting despite her arthritis. Private worry: she is beginning to lose words — not dramatically, just occasionally — and she is racing against her own mind to pass on what she knows.
characters.terrified_by: Dying before she can tell Tayak the one thing that changes everything — and Tayak finding it in the dirt instead, cold and without context.
characters.humiliated_by: Being treated as a relic or a symbol rather than a person with agency and a specific, consequential history.
characters.made_happy_by: Hearing Tayak say, out loud, in a public forum, the names of the ancestors Nora taught her.
characters.dramatic_question: Will Nora finally tell Tayak the full truth about the mound — including the oral history she has kept since her own grandmother told it to her in 1962 — before the excavation makes the truth irrelevant?
characters.off_axis_attribute: Nora is warm and funny in company but has a cold, absolute ruthlessness when she believes the tribe's survival is at stake — she once reported a tribal member to state authorities to prevent him from selling land, and she has never apologized for it.

characters.name: Garrett Slade
characters.role: Antagonist; Maryland State Historic Preservation Officer
characters.archetype: The bureaucrat as weapon — a man who genuinely believes in the rules he enforces and is therefore more dangerous than a corrupt villain.
characters.description: 55, white, third-generation Marylander whose own family farm sits two miles from the mound. Runs marathons. Has a daughter, Elena, who is a tribal rights attorney in New Mexico, a fact he mentions too often. Reads history obsessively but only published history. Private worry: he suspects his own family's land title has a gap in it from the 1680s that he has never investigated.
characters.terrified_by: The discovery that his family's land was taken directly from the people whose mound he is now processing through a state system.
characters.humiliated_by: Being shown, in public, that his procedural correctness produced a morally indefensible outcome.
characters.made_happy_by: Finding a procedural pathway that lets him do the right thing without admitting the system was wrong.
characters.dramatic_question: Will Slade's faith in institutional process survive the moment he realizes the process itself is the instrument of erasure?
characters.off_axis_attribute: Slade is not racist in any obvious way; he has published sympathetic papers on Indigenous land rights and genuinely admires Tayak's scholarship. His antagonism is structural: he believes the process must be followed, and following the process will destroy the mound.

characters.name: Marcus Redcloud
characters.role: Tribal council chair; Tayak's political ally and occasional obstacle
characters.archetype: The politician who has made too many compromises and knows it.
characters.description: 52, Piscataway, grew up in Prince George's County. Law degree from Howard. Coaches youth lacrosse on weekends. Drinks too much coffee and not enough water. Has known Tayak since she was a teenager and feels a complicated mix of pride and guilt about how hard her life has been.
characters.terrified_by: Losing the recognition fight after everything — after all the compromises, all the years, all the things he told himself were temporary.
characters.humiliated_by: Having his private compromise exposed to the tribal community he has spent thirty years serving.
characters.made_happy_by: Watching the tribe's children stand on recognized land and know it is theirs.
characters.dramatic_question: Will Marcus use his undisclosed leverage to save the mound, even though doing so will expose the compromise he has hidden from his own people?
characters.off_axis_attribute: Marcus is an effective advocate in rooms Tayak can't enter, but he has a private agreement with a real estate developer that he has not disclosed to the tribe — not corrupt exactly, but a hedge, a backup plan, a thing he tells himself he will never use.

characters.name: Dr. Elliot Voss
characters.role: Tayak's department chair; scientific establishment voice
characters.archetype: The gatekeeper who believes he is a guardian.
characters.description: 62, white, Harvard PhD. Has a famous monograph on Chesapeake pre-contact trade networks that Tayak's work is quietly dismantling. Plays classical guitar badly. Genuinely fond of Tayak in the way a person is fond of a protégé they have not fully understood.
characters.terrified_by: The university withdrawing his lab's federal grant over the political controversy Tayak's excavation generates.
characters.humiliated_by: Having his monograph publicly corrected by the very student he mentored.
characters.made_happy_by: Being cited in the final heritage report — even a footnote would do.
characters.dramatic_question: Will Voss choose institutional protection or genuine advocacy when Tayak's findings put the university's federal funding relationship at risk?
characters.off_axis_attribute: Voss has spent his career championing Indigenous archaeology in the abstract while consistently failing specific Indigenous archaeologists in the particular — and he has a gift for framing each failure as being for their own good.

characters.name: Kimi Moyaone
characters.role: Tayak's younger cousin; tribal youth activist and digital media organizer
characters.archetype: The next generation who refuses to wait.
characters.description: 26, lives in DC, works remotely as a UX designer. Runs a tribal heritage social media account with 80,000 followers. Learned beadwork from Nora. Has a boyfriend Tayak has never met. Private worry: she suspects she is more useful to the cause as a symbol than as a person, and she is not sure how she feels about that.
characters.terrified_by: Losing Nora before she has learned everything Nora knows.
characters.humiliated_by: Being told her activism is hurting the very cause she loves.
characters.made_happy_by: Seeing the mound's story told in the tribe's own words, not filtered through a state report.
characters.dramatic_question: Will Kimi's public campaign save the mound or destroy Tayak's legal case by making the excavation a media circus before the evidence is secure?
characters.off_axis_attribute: Kimi is brilliant at mobilizing public attention but has a reckless streak — she will post something true but strategically catastrophic if she believes it needs to be said, and she does not always consult the people it will affect.

characters.name: Wren Calvert
characters.role: Tayak's graduate student field assistant; scientific conscience
characters.archetype: The true believer in archaeological method who is slowly radicalized by what she witnesses.
characters.description: 28, PhD candidate. Meticulous field notes. Runs a small Etsy shop selling hand-drawn artifact illustrations. Reads Victorian novels for comfort. Has a complicated relationship with her mother, who thinks archaeology is a waste of a good brain.
characters.terrified_by: That her presence on this dig — a white woman from a land-owning Virginia family — is itself a form of the problem.
characters.humiliated_by: Being exposed as complicit in the very history she came to study.
characters.made_happy_by: Producing field documentation so thorough and so beautiful that it cannot be dismissed or ignored.
characters.dramatic_question: Will Wren's discovery about her own family's connection to the Piscataway dispossession force her to choose between her mentor's cause and her own family's legal interests?
characters.off_axis_attribute: Wren is white, from a wealthy Virginia family, and chose Indigenous archaeology specifically to atone for something she will not name — a family history she has researched but never confronted directly.

characters.name: Siosaia (called Saya)
characters.role: Past-timeline POV character; Stratum One ancestor, 1690s
characters.archetype: The survivor who must choose between compliance and resistance when both paths lead to loss.
characters.description: Late 20s, Piscataway, daughter of a community leader. Speaks English and some Dutch from trading contacts. Has a husband, Okwi, who is a skilled canoe-builder and deeply skeptical of her legal strategy. Has a young daughter she is teaching to read. The glass trade bead Tayak finds in Stratum One belonged to Saya — it was a gift from a Lenape trading partner and the only thing she kept from her own mother.
characters.terrified_by: That the petition she is drafting will be used as evidence of submission rather than assertion.
characters.humiliated_by: Being treated as a supplicant in a legal system she understands better than the men administering it.
characters.made_happy_by: Hearing her daughter recite the names of their ancestors in the correct order, without prompting.
characters.dramatic_question: Can Saya use the colonial legal system to protect her people's claim to the mound land before the new governor's land grants extinguish it — and at what cost to herself and her family?
characters.off_axis_attribute: Saya is the most politically astute person in her community — she reads colonial legal documents better than most colonists — but she is constitutionally incapable of performing deference, which makes every negotiation she enters a near-disaster she has to rescue with her own intelligence.

characters.name: Okwi
characters.role: Past-timeline secondary POV character; Saya's husband, 1690s
characters.archetype: The man who builds things and watches them be taken — a craftsman whose skill cannot protect what he loves.
characters.description: Early 30s. Builds the finest canoes on the Potomac watershed. Teaches young men the craft. Has a dry, dark humor that Saya finds infuriating and irresistible. The oilskin document Tayak finds in Stratum One is Saya's petition; Okwi is the one who wrapped it and buried it at the mound when the petition failed.
characters.terrified_by: That his children will grow up believing the colonial system is legitimate.
characters.humiliated_by: Being made to watch his community lose land through a process he was never permitted to participate in.
characters.made_happy_by: Standing in a canoe on the Potomac at dawn, with no one else in sight.
characters.dramatic_question: Will Okwi's refusal to engage with the colonial legal process undermine Saya's petition, or will his act of physical defiance at the mound become the event that forces the colonial assembly to take the petition seriously?
characters.off_axis_attribute: Okwi is patient and methodical in everything except his contempt for compromise, which is absolute and occasionally violent — he once broke a colonial trader's measuring scale with his bare hands and spent three days in a stockade for it, and he considers those three days well spent.

characters.name: Matta
characters.role: Past-timeline POV character; Stratum Two ancestor, 1740s
characters.archetype: The keeper of ceremony in a world that has criminalized ceremony.
characters.description: 50s, Piscataway, grandson of Saya and Okwi. Has lived his entire life under colonial governance and has developed a sophisticated double life. Makes the finest ceramic pipes in the region. Has a granddaughter, Tessa, he is training as his successor.
characters.terrified_by: That his granddaughter will not be able to find the buried objects after he is gone.
characters.humiliated_by: Being forced to perform Christianity for colonial observers while his own people watch.
characters.made_happy_by: The moment in a ceremony when the room stops being afraid and becomes, briefly, itself.
characters.dramatic_question: Will Matta's decision to bury the community's ceremonial objects in the mound preserve the tradition or end it, since only he and his granddaughter know where everything is buried?
characters.off_axis_attribute: Matta is genuinely devout and genuinely funny — he uses humor as a liturgical tool, believing that laughter opens the same door as prayer, which makes him beloved by his community and deeply suspicious to the colonial missionaries.

characters.name: Tessa (Tessahki)
characters.archetype: The inheritor who must reconstruct what was hidden before she was ready to receive it.
characters.description: Teenager to young adult across her arc. Learns the ceramic craft from Matta. Has a colonial-educated brother who has converted and with whom she has a painful, loving, irresolvable argument that lasts their entire lives. The shell gorget Tayak finds in Stratum Three was Tessa's.
