characters.terrified_by: That she has misremembered the burial map and the objects are lost.
characters.humiliated_by: Being told by her brother that her ceremonies are superstition and her grief is ignorance.
characters.made_happy_by: Finding the buried objects exactly where Matta said they would be.
characters.dramatic_question: After Matta dies without fully passing on the burial map, can Tessa reconstruct the mound's interior from fragments of memory and partial instruction — and will the reconstruction be accurate enough to matter?
characters.off_axis_attribute: Tessa has a photographic memory for spatial relationships but is emotionally opaque to herself, unable to name what she feels until long after she has acted on it.

characters.era: circa 1200 CE, Woodland Period, Chesapeake region
characters.name: Ahanu
characters.role: Past-timeline POV character; Stratum Four ancestor, circa 1200 CE
characters.archetype: The leader who must hold a community together through a crisis that has no political solution — only a spiritual one.
characters.description: 40s, community leader by practice not title. Has three adult children, two considering leaving. Has a rival, Sokan, who believes the drought is punishment for the community's failure to maintain the old ways — and who is not entirely wrong.
characters.terrified_by: That her children will leave and the community will dissolve quietly, one family at a time.
characters.humiliated_by: Being told by Sokan, in front of the community, that her leadership has failed.
characters.made_happy_by: Rain. Actual rain, after a long dry season.
characters.dramatic_question: Can Ahanu hold her community together through a prolonged drought — and will the ceremony she leads at the mound be enough to restore not the rain but the people's willingness to stay?
characters.off_axis_attribute: Ahanu is a gifted orator and a poor listener — she can move a crowd to tears and then completely miss what the person standing next to her actually needs.

characters.name: Sokan
characters.role: Past-timeline secondary POV character; Ahanu's rival, circa 1200 CE
characters.archetype: The traditionalist who is right about the diagnosis and wrong about the cure.
characters.description: 50s, keeper of the oldest ceremonial traditions. Has been right about three community crises in a row and has never let anyone forget it. Has a daughter, Waya, who is Ahanu's closest friend. The antler figure Tayak finds in Stratum Five was carved by Sokan and given to Ahanu as a gesture of reconciliation after the drought broke.
characters.terrified_by: That the old ways will be lost not through force but through the community's own exhaustion.
characters.humiliated_by: Being shown that his certainty caused harm.
characters.made_happy_by: Watching a young person perform a ceremony correctly, without being told how.
characters.dramatic_question: Will Sokan's insistence on the old ways at any cost fracture the community he is trying to save — and will he recognize, in time, that Ahanu's adaptation is not betrayal but survival?
characters.off_axis_attribute: Sokan is genuinely wise about the community's spiritual failures and genuinely cruel about the people he holds responsible — he has a gift for identifying real problems and then making them worse by the way he names them.

characters.name: Waya
characters.role: Past-timeline POV character; Sokan's daughter and Ahanu's friend, circa 1200–1220 CE
characters.archetype: The person caught between two people she loves who are destroying each other.
characters.description: 30s. Has a husband and two young children. Teaches her children to hunt. Has a private grief: a third child who died in the drought's worst year, a loss she has not spoken of to anyone. The copper pendant Tayak finds in Stratum Five was Waya's, passed to her by Ahanu.
characters.terrified_by: That her father and Ahanu will both die without reconciling.
characters.humiliated_by: Being used as a messenger between her father and Ahanu rather than consulted as a person.
characters.made_happy_by: A morning hunt alone in the forest, before anyone needs anything from her.
characters.dramatic_question: Can Waya broker a reconciliation between her father and Ahanu before the drought-driven fracture becomes permanent — and what will it cost her to be the bridge between two people who both love her and neither of whom will compromise?
characters.off_axis_attribute: Waya is the community's best hunter but is constitutionally unable to track the emotional states of the people closest to her — always the last to know when a relationship has broken.

characters.era: circa 500 CE, Late Archaic / Early Woodland transition
characters.name: Kessik
characters.role: Past-timeline POV character; Stratum Six ancestor, circa 500 CE
characters.archetype: The innovator who introduces the deliberate burial mound to a community that has never built one.
characters.description: 30s, community leader's daughter. Has traveled farther than anyone in her community and seen mounds built by communities to the north and west. Has a younger brother, Pell, who thinks the mound project is a waste of labor and says so loudly.
characters.terrified_by: That she will die before the mound is finished and no one will complete it.
characters.humiliated_by: Being told her vision is impractical by people who have never tried to see past the next season.
characters.made_happy_by: The moment the community agrees — not because she persuaded them, but because they understood.
characters.dramatic_question: Can Kessik persuade her community to build the mound — a project that will take years and offer no immediate practical benefit — by making them understand that the mound is not for the dead but for the living who will come after?
characters.off_axis_attribute: Kessik is visionary and charismatic but has a catastrophizing mind — always three disasters ahead of the present moment, which makes her an excellent planner and an exhausting companion.

characters.name: Pell
characters.role: Past-timeline secondary POV character; Kessik's brother, circa 500 CE
characters.archetype: The skeptic who becomes the mound's most devoted builder.
characters.description: Late 20s. Strongest person in the community by a significant margin. Has a gift for structural problem-solving. Has a wife, Nima, who understood the mound's purpose before he did and has been quietly waiting for him to catch up.
characters.terrified_by: That his sister will die thinking he never believed in her.
characters.humiliated_by: Being wrong about something he argued loudly against.
characters.made_happy_by: Solving a structural problem that everyone else said was impossible.
characters.dramatic_question: Will Pell's conversion from skeptic to builder come in time to save the project when Kessik falls ill and cannot lead it?
characters.off_axis_attribute: Pell's skepticism is not laziness — it is a deep, almost philosophical suspicion of anything that cannot be immediately tested, which makes him the community's best engineer and its worst visionary.

characters.era: circa 100 BC, Early Woodland / Hopewell-influenced, Chesapeake region
characters.name: Yanu
characters.role: Past-timeline POV character; the founding ancestor, circa 100 BC
characters.archetype: The woman who makes the first act — who buries the first object in the earth that will become the mound, and in doing so invents the tradition that will last two thousand years.
characters.description: Late 30s. Has four living children and one dead one — a daughter, Taya, who died in her second year. The copper pendant was made for Taya by a Hopewell-connected trader. Has a husband, Ranu, who grieves differently — loudly, communally. Has a gift for reading weather from birds.
characters.terrified_by: That Taya will be forgotten — that in two generations no one will remember her name.
characters.humiliated_by: Having her grief treated as a public event rather than a private one.
characters.made_happy_by: Hearing one of her living children say Taya's name without being prompted.
characters.dramatic_question: Will Yanu's private act of burial — placing her daughter's copper pendant in the earth and speaking her daughter's name — become the founding act of a tradition she cannot foresee, and will she live long enough to understand what she has started?
characters.off_axis_attribute: Yanu is not a leader, a shaman, or a chief — she is a mother who has just lost a child, and the burial is not a political act or a spiritual ceremony but a private act of grief that her community, watching her, recognizes as something larger than grief and begins to imitate.

characters.name: Ranu
characters.role: Past-timeline secondary POV character; Yanu's husband, circa 100 BC
characters.archetype: The man who grieves loudly and loves quietly — who does not understand his wife's silence but follows her to the burial site anyway.
characters.description: 40s. Tells stories at every communal gathering. Has a reputation for embellishment that is both celebrated and distrusted. Carves small figures from antler as a meditative practice — the figures he makes after Taya's death are simpler, more still.
characters.terrified_by: That his embellishments have made him untrustworthy at the moment when the truth most needs to be told.
characters.humiliated_by: Being unable to tell the one story that matters most.
characters.made_happy_by: An audience that is completely still — not entertained, but genuinely moved.
characters.dramatic_question: Will Ranu find a way to tell Taya's story — to make the private burial Yanu performed into a community memory — without violating the privacy Yanu needs?
characters.off_axis_attribute: Ranu is the community's storyteller but has never been able to tell the story of his own daughter's death, and this failure haunts him more than the death itself.

characters.name: Ida Moyaone
characters.archetype: The keeper of the chain — the woman who received the oral history from her own grandmother and held it for forty years before passing it to Nora.
characters.description: Born 1898, died 1964. Taught elementary school for thirty years. Kept a private journal she never showed anyone. Made quilts using patterns her own grandmother taught her. Told Nora the family's oral history on a single night in 1962, two years before she died, because she had run out of time to wait for the right moment.
characters.terrified_by: That the story will die with her because she waited too long to tell it.
characters.humiliated_by: Being told by a BIA official that her people's oral traditions are folklore, not history.
characters.made_happy_by: Nora repeating back to her, word for word, what she has just been told.
characters.dramatic_question: Will Ida pass the full oral history to Nora before the pressures of mid-century assimilation — the BIA termination policy, the suburban expansion of Charles County, her own family's desire to survive by disappearing — make the story too dangerous to tell?
characters.off_axis_attribute: Ida is the most formally educated woman in her family's history — a schoolteacher with a college certificate — and she has spent her life in a painful negotiation between the written record she was trained to trust and the spoken record she was raised to carry, never fully believing either.

outline.wow_factor: Every artifact Tayak unearths unlocks a fully dramatized past-timeline chapter reached through the chain of oral tradition — a grandmother's story about her grandmother's story about her grandmother's story — so the reader descends through two millennia of complete, named, lived lives carried entirely in spoken words, and the novel's central revelation (that Tayak is excavating her own family's ground) arrives not as a supernatural flash but as the slow, devastating accumulation of a story that was always being told, just never to her.
outline.story_arc_name: The Descent: Seven Strata, Seven Centuries, One Family — and the Two-Thousand-Year Answer Carried in Spoken Words
outline.dramatic_question: Can Dr. Tayak Moyaone prove her people's unbroken presence on this land before the state seizes the burial mound — and will the chain of oral stories her grandmother has kept, each one dramatizing a real ancestor's life going back to 100 BC, constitute the proof that no court, no institution, and no act of erasure can finally destroy?
